The closing condition then turns a doctrine into a question about actual practice.

crossReferences.why: Reports a people found prostrating to the sun instead of God, doing exactly what this line forbids.
Reasons from the setting of star, moon and sun to the one who made them, reaching this ayah's conclusion by argument.
Places the sun and moon among those who themselves prostrate to God, settling their standing in one clause.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once this week at a moment you can name in advance, first light or the minute the sun goes down, and stand still for its whole length without your phone. Do not try to feel anything. Just watch something you depend on and did not make, and notice you have arranged the entire day around it without once looking.

studies.title: The Land Stirs And Swells
studies.meaning: The first line answers pride with indifference. If they are too proud to bow, the bowing continues elsewhere without them, night and day, by beings who never grow bored of it. Then the argument drops to ground level. You have seen land lying flat and finished, and you have seen what water does to it within days. Commentators treat this as a premise rather than an image: the one who did that to the earth will do it to the dead. The reasoning runs from something already witnessed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's run of signs before it turns to those who twist the revelation. Resurrection was the claim the Meccans found hardest to take, and the Quran answers it again and again from agriculture rather than from abstract argument. The audience lived where rain was rare enough to count as an event and its effect on dead ground was fast and dramatic. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for the boredom of doing one thing too long, not physical exhaustion. It occurs in this form only here, and it answers an objection about endless worship that nobody would raise aloud.
A word used elsewhere of downcast eyes and lowered faces. Applied to land it describes a posture rather than a measurement, ground that has given up and flattened itself.
A verb for a shudder running through something. Paired with the swelling that follows, it gives the ground a movement you could stand and watch rather than a condition you could only infer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In the Hijaz rain arrived in short violent bursts and the dry valleys ran for hours. Within a week ground that had been bare stone and dust carried green, and grazing appeared where there had been nothing to graze. Herders moved on news of rainfall days away, and whole seasons turned on where a storm had crossed. Nobody listening needed the process explained; they had organised their lives around it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the still land here is used elsewhere in the Quran for human beings on the Day of Resurrection, their eyes lowered and downcast. In this exact form it occurs three times, and only this one is about ground. The same posture is given to dead earth before rain and to people before judgement, in a passage that then says one of the two will be revived.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues for resurrection by analogy from something the audience already accepts without noticing. Nobody finds spring implausible, and the claim is that its implausibility is of exactly the same kind. It also deals with pride by refusing it a stage. The refusal of those who will not bow changes nothing at all, and the surah does not argue with them. It simply reports what continues elsewhere.

crossReferences.why: Runs the identical image of barren earth stirring and swelling, and draws the same conclusion about raising the dead.
Ends the same comparison with the word resurrection, making the link between rainfall and rising explicit.
Describes the same tireless worship by those near your Lord, at the close of another surah, and is itself a place of prostration.

studies.applyIt: Find one dead-looking patch you walk past, a verge, a cracked pot, a strip beside a car park, and look at it deliberately twice, a month apart. Put a note in your calendar now for the second look. This ayah asks you to witness a change rather than to believe in one, and the witnessing needs an appointment.

studies.title: Do As You Please
studies.meaning: Three moves in one line. First, those who twist the signs are told they are not concealed, which answers a hope nobody had voiced. Then a question with no verdict attached: is the one hurled into the Fire better, or the one who arrives secure. The second man is described by his safety rather than by any deed listed for him. Last comes a permission that is not one. Do as you please is the phrasing of someone who has finished arguing and is content to let the outcome speak.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been laying out signs and answering objections for forty lines, and this is where the argument stops rather than concludes. Commentators read the closing imperative as addressed to people who had already refused everything on offer. The setting is the later Meccan years, when the leadership's position had hardened and persuasion had visibly reached its limit. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for turning something aside from straight, related to the word for the side-niche cut into a grave wall. Used of the signs, it describes distortion rather than open denial.
From the root behind faith and trust. The second man is defined by the safety he arrives in rather than by anything he did, so the contrast is between two conditions.

A plain imperative, used here stripped of the encouragement it usually carries. Classical readers take it as a warning shaped like permission, a recognised device in Arabic speech rather than an invitation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic had a word for the side-chamber cut into the wall of a grave, and it comes from the same root as the verb for deviating used here. Burial in the Hijaz was quick and shallow, and that niche was the ordinary form. The vocabulary of turning aside was therefore not abstract for the first listeners. It belonged to digging, and to something everyone had stood and watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for twisting the signs occurs three times in the Quran. One of the other two concerns people who distort the names of God. The third appears where opponents claimed a foreign speaker lay behind the recitation, and there it describes the direction they were inclining in. Deviation in this vocabulary is consistently a matter of language.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah sets out the two possible ends of a life and refuses to weigh them for the listener. It states them as a question and moves on, which treats the reader as capable of answering. It also pairs being seen with being free. The permission to act as you wish is genuine, and so is the final clause. Neither cancels the other, and the passage is content to hold both.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of those who distort the names of God, showing the word's other application in the Quran.
Gives the same kind of permission in the same tone, followed immediately by consequence rather than by further argument.
Describes those who arrive secure from the terror of that Day, matching the second figure in this ayah.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you keep doing that you have quietly decided is nobody's business. Do not stop it today. Instead describe it in one plain sentence to yourself, the way you would describe someone else's habit. The permission in this ayah is real, and so is its last clause. Most of the work lies in refusing to phrase it kindly.

studies.title: Falsehood Cannot Reach It
studies.meaning: The sentence about those who reject the Reminder is left unfinished, with no consequence stated. Commentators explain that the threat is implied and the attention deliberately shifts to what was rejected. It is called a book that cannot be overcome, then guarded from two directions at once, before it and behind it. The pair is read as meaning every direction, or earlier and later scripture, or wording and meaning. The passage ends by naming its source rather than defending its contents.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's final movement, after the opponents' tactic of drowning out the recitation has already been quoted a few lines earlier. What is claimed here concerns the text's own durability, and it is addressed to people who expected the movement to fade as others had. No occasion is reported; the passage belongs to the surah's sustained argument about the standing of the recitation.

keyTerms.note: One of the Quran's names for itself, from the root for remembering and for mentioning aloud. It frames the revelation as something restored to people rather than newly introduced to them.
A word for what cannot be reached or overpowered, used of a fortified place and of a person too strong to touch. It is also, elsewhere, one of the names of God.
The opposite of what is true and established, but carrying hollowness rather than error. Its root means to be void, so what is excluded here is emptiness dressed up as content.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was the archive of Arabia and it travelled by memory, which made tampering a live risk. Verses were misattributed, lines inserted, whole poems claimed by rival tribes. Reciters were judged partly on their reliability as transmitters, and arguments about who really composed a famous line could run for generations. A claim that a text could not be got at from any side was one that audience understood practically.
studies.didYouKnow: The word here translated as invincible is one of God's own names elsewhere in the Quran, where it occurs in this exact form more than twenty times, usually paired with wisdom or might. Applying it to the Book hands the revelation an attribute the text otherwise reserves for its source, without any explanation of the transfer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds the Quran's authority in its origin rather than in any institution that carries it. Falsehood is excluded not by a promise of human vigilance but by a description of the one who sent it down, named as wise and as praiseworthy. That second name matters. Wisdom on its own would be competence; praiseworthiness says the source is worth what is being claimed for the text.

crossReferences.why: Names the same Reminder and states outright the preservation that this passage implies without ever saying it.
Offers a test for the claim, inviting readers to search the text for the discrepancy said to be absent.
Puts the same unassailability as an open challenge rather than a description, addressed to humans and jinn together.

studies.applyIt: Take one short passage you think you already know and read it slowly enough to notice a word you have been skating over. Look that single word up. The claim made here is that the text holds under pressure. You can only find that out by pressing somewhere, and one word is enough to begin with.

studies.title: Nothing New Is Being Said
studies.meaning: The consolation offered is an unusual one. Not that the abuse will stop, but that it is not original. Whatever is being said to you was said to the messengers before you. Commentators take it as covering the accusations, and on a second reading the revelation itself, since the same message came earlier. The line then closes with two attributes held together, forgiveness and painful consequence, and neither is softened by the presence of the other.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing section of a surah addressed to a Prophet under sustained public ridicule in his own city. Commentators place the consolation in the later Meccan years, once the opposition had become organised. No specific occasion is reported. The ayah belongs to a pattern across the Meccan surahs, where the histories of earlier prophets are supplied as reassurance rather than as history.

keyTerms.note: The verb is passive and the speakers go unnamed. Leaving them out reduces the opposition from particular personalities to a repeating phenomenon, which is the whole comfort the line has to offer.
From a root meaning to cover or shield, used of a helmet. Forgiveness here is less the erasure of a deed than something laid over it so that it no longer exposes the person.
From the root for a heel and for what follows behind. The word carries the sense of something arriving after an act, as its tail, rather than being handed down arbitrarily.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Mecca was maintained by talk. A man's standing rose and fell in the assemblies where poets traded insults and traders traded news, and a sustained campaign of mockery could damage a family's prospects in the markets. There was no answering it except by outlasting it or by force. Being told that others had faced identical talk was a specific kind of relief in that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of possessing forgiveness with possessing painful consequence occurs in this exact double construction in only one other place in the Quran, in a surah that likewise answers people demanding the punishment be hurried along. In both, the two attributes stand inside a single clause with nothing between them to rank one above the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to let either attribute be the final word about God. Forgiveness is stated first, which readers have long noticed, but the second is not withdrawn afterwards. Holding both without resolution is itself the claim being made: a God reducible to one of them would be easier to predict and easier to manage. The ayah leaves a reader able to do neither, and treats that as the correct position.

crossReferences.why: Sets the same two attributes side by side in one sentence, answering people who wanted the punishment brought forward.
Gives the same pair as a two-part announcement the Prophet is instructed to deliver to God's servants.
Turns this consolation into an instruction, pointing back to the endurance of the resolute among earlier messengers.

studies.applyIt: Think of the criticism that gets under your skin fastest, then name one other person who has heard the identical thing. Not a famous example, someone you actually know. This ayah does not tell you the criticism is false. It tells you that you are not the first address it was sent to, and that changes how heavily it sits.

studies.title: Guidance And Healing Or Deafness
studies.meaning: A hypothetical is used to show that an objection could never have been satisfied. Had the revelation arrived in a language they did not know, they would have complained that it was not made clear; as it is, in their own tongue, they complain anyway. The Arabic word for foreign also covers speech that is hard to follow, so both the objection and its answer turn on clarity. The second half then divides listeners by what happens inside them rather than by what they say.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's name comes from the claim in its opening ayat that the signs of this Book are set out in detail, and this passage defends that claim against a particular charge. Objectors in Mecca disputed the message's source, its language and the standing of the man delivering it. The reply here takes the language complaint and tests it by imagining the alternative they say they wanted.

keyTerms.note: One word covering both a non-Arabic language and speech that cannot be followed. The two senses are not separated in Arabic, which is exactly what makes the objection in this ayah collapse.
The word for recovery from illness, not for comfort. Applied to a text, it describes something that repairs a condition rather than something that explains a situation or improves a mood.
A weight in the ear rather than an absence of hearing. The same root gives words for a heavy load, so what is described is obstruction by something present rather than a faculty missing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca heard many languages during the trading season, and Arabs used a single word for anyone whose speech they could not follow, whether foreign or simply unclear. Poetry contests judged clarity as a virtue and obscurity as failure, and audiences were expert listeners. A message arriving in the poets' own idiom removed in advance the excuse a foreign one would have handed them.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah's name comes from a verb in its third ayah, describing a Book whose signs are set out in detail. That same verb reappears here inside the objectors' imagined complaint, where they would have asked why its signs were not set out in detail. The surah is named after a word it also places in the mouth of its opponents.
studies.theologicalSignificance: One text is said to do two opposite things depending on who receives it, which locates the difference in the hearing rather than in the message, and does not treat that as a defect in either. The closing image is worded with care. They are being called from a distant place, so the calling has not stopped and is not withdrawn; what has changed is the distance across which it has to travel.

crossReferences.why: States the same double effect: healing and mercy for some, and an increase only in loss for others.
Names the same word for healing, and locates what is being healed in the chests rather than the mind.
Contains the phrase this ayah echoes, a Book whose signs are set out in detail in Arabic.

studies.applyIt: Think of one objection you have raised recently to something you did not want to do. Ask yourself, honestly, what you would have said if that objection had been fully answered. If another one arrives immediately, you have learned something about the first. This ayah runs exactly that test and lets the answer stand on its own.

studies.title: The Book They Argued Over
studies.meaning: A precedent is offered without comment. Moses was given the Book and disagreement broke out over it, exactly as it has now. A prior word from the Lord is the only reason judgement has not already been passed, and commentators read that word as the decision to defer the reckoning to a set time. Then the frame narrows sharply. Good work is for the one who does it, harm falls on the one who does it, and the last clause rules out injustice at the source.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just described the recitation being met with heaviness in the ears, and the mention of Moses places that reception inside a pattern rather than treating it as new. Commentators note that the Quran repeatedly raises earlier scripture in Meccan contexts to show that dispute over revelation is old. No occasion is reported for either ayah in this pair.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb from the root for following behind one another. Disagreement in Arabic is pictured as parties standing at each other's backs, and the passive form here names no side as responsible.
An intensive form describing doubt that will not resolve. It is doubt that keeps a person restless rather than doubt that drives inquiry, which is why the passage treats it as a condition.
An intensive form of the word for a wrongdoer, the shape Arabic uses for someone who does a thing habitually. Denying the intensive is read as ruling out injustice at any scale at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca knew about scriptural communities. Jewish and Christian traders passed through, monks lived along the Syrian route, and Abyssinia across the water was a Christian kingdom Meccan merchants dealt with directly. The Quraysh had heard that people of earlier books argued among themselves about them. Raising Moses here appealed to something the audience could check rather than something they had to take on trust.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing phrase denying injustice uses an intensive form, the shape Arabic reserves for someone who does a thing constantly or in great quantity. This exact wording occurs four times in the Quran and always in that intensive form, never in the plain one, which readers of Arabic have long found worth pausing over since the plain denial would seem the stronger statement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two lines set a communal fact against an individual one. Communities dispute, and the dispute is not settled on schedule; that is the first. Nothing about the delay changes where a deed lands; that is the second. Together they leave the reader without a reason to wait for the argument to close before acting, because the account being kept is already personal and is not waiting for anything.

crossReferences.why: Traces the same emergence of dispute over revelation, and names the clear knowledge that had arrived before it.
Uses the identical clause about a prior word from your Lord deferring judgement between people who differ.
Extends the second line's principle, keeping each account with the one who made it and no other.

studies.applyIt: Notice a disagreement you have been treating as a reason to hold off, about a community, a teacher, a question you have not resolved. Ask whether anything you would do today actually depends on settling it. Usually one small thing does not. Do that thing while the argument stays open, since the second half of this passage is about the part already yours.

studies.title: No Fruit Leaves Its Sheath
studies.meaning: A question about the Hour is answered by refusing it and then widening it. Knowledge of the Hour goes back to Him, and so does the emergence of every fruit from its covering, and every conception and delivery. The examples chosen are all hidden processes with public results, which is precisely the shape of the Hour itself. Then the scene jumps forward. He calls out asking where His associates are, and the reply is a confession: not one of us will testify to that now.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Questions about when the Hour would arrive were a standing challenge from the Quraysh, and the Quran answers them repeatedly by relocating the question rather than supplying a date. Commentators treat the pairing here as deliberate: an unanswered question about timing, followed at once by a scene in which the timing has stopped mattering. No occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The green spathe a date cluster or a bud pushes out of. The word appears only here in this form, and it names a covering that exists in order to be broken from the inside.
Partners in a share, from the vocabulary of joint ownership in trade. Attaching the possessive to God makes the phrase deliberately strange, quoting the claim back to the people who made it.
From the root for the ear and for granting permission. The verb means to make something formally known, so the confession arrives in the register of an announcement rather than a plea.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date palms were the wealth of the oases, and everything about them was watched. The sheath swelled for weeks before it split and the flower cluster emerged, and a grower could read the coming season from it. Pregnancies in the household and in the herd were followed the same way, with attention and no certainty. Both examples name the exact places where that life waited on an outcome it could not hurry.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the sheath used here occurs only in this ayah in this form. A related form appears once more, in a short surah that names the date palm with its sheaths among the things set out for creation alongside grain and fragrant herbs. Between them, the whole Quranic vocabulary for the covering on a date cluster amounts to two words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage ties a doctrine about divine knowledge to processes the reader can watch. Knowledge is not asserted as a general attribute; it is located in the sheath and the womb, places where outcomes stay hidden and then arrive. That makes the unanswered question about the Hour easier to sit with. And the confession at the end shows the associates were never a position anyone could defend, only one that held while nobody asked.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same reserved knowledge, again pairing the Hour with what is carried in a womb and with tomorrow.
Runs the same argument from small hidden events, down to a falling leaf, up to knowledge of everything.
Records the question this ayah answers, and gives the same refusal to name a date for it.

studies.applyIt: Choose one thing you are waiting on and have no control over: a result, a decision someone else is making, a recovery. Write down the date you expect to know by, then put the note away. This ayah does not promise the answer sooner. It asks you to notice you have been treating not knowing as a fault rather than as a condition.

studies.title: What Deserts You And What Does Not
studies.meaning: Two things happen at once in the first line. What these people used to call on wanders off from them, and the realisation lands that there is nowhere left to duck aside to. Then the passage turns from that scene to ordinary human beings, and the observation is about stamina. Nobody ever tires of asking for good. But when harm touches, the same person collapses into hopelessness. Commentators present the imbalance as a fact about people rather than as a charge against them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is drawing to a close and moves out of the judgement scene into a portrait of the human being that runs for several ayat. Commentators read this stretch as addressed to everyone and not only to the surah's opponents, since the pattern described is common to all. No occasion is reported. The setting remains a city where calling on lesser powers for rain, trade and children was routine.

keyTerms.note: The verb usually rendered as going astray. Applied to the things people prayed to, it makes them the ones who get lost, which reverses the accusation those same people had been making.
From a root for dodging around an obstacle. It names not safety but the sideways movement that avoids a blow, and that movement is what this line reports has gone.
An intensive form occurring only here in the Quran. Arabic separates it from ordinary despair by its finality: not the loss of one hope but a settled conviction that none is on offer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prayer for good things was constant and specific in Arabia. People asked for rain, for a safe caravan, for a son, for a debt to be released, and they asked at shrines, before idols, and at the graves of ancestors. The asking never stopped because the needs never did. What this passage adds is the other half of the pattern, equally visible: how quickly a household fell silent when a caravan failed to return.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for total hopelessness at the end of this passage occurs nowhere else in the Quran in this form. The word standing beside it for despair is common by comparison, so the sentence stacks a familiar term against a rare intensive one. The effect in Arabic is a description that keeps going past the point where the expected vocabulary would have stopped.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats despair as a failure of consistency rather than a failure of nerve. Someone who asks constantly in good times has already conceded that there is a listener; the collapse when things go wrong is therefore a change of belief and not merely of mood. Naming it as a pattern rather than a sin leaves the reader room to recognise themselves without being condemned by the recognition.

crossReferences.why: Names despair as the one thing believers are told not to fall into, spoken by Jacob to his sons.
Answers the same collapse directly, addressed to those who have gone furthest against themselves and still have room.
Runs the same disappearance of other objects of prayer, set at sea in the moment of danger rather than at judgement.

studies.applyIt: The next time something goes badly, notice how long it takes before you stop asking for anything at all. Set the bar low: one sentence, out loud, on the day it happens. This passage is not asking you to feel hopeful. It is pointing out that the asking stops first and the feeling follows it down, in that order.

studies.title: He Says This Is Mine
studies.meaning: Relief arrives after hardship and the man immediately explains it. This is mine, he says, meaning it was owed to him or produced by him. Two further claims follow in the same breath: he doubts the Hour is coming at all, and yet if he were returned to his Lord he would certainly have the very best there. Commentators point out that the contradiction is left standing. He denies the reckoning and assumes he would do well in it, which is what entitlement sounds like out loud.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, part of the surah's closing portrait of the human being under changing conditions. Commentators connect it directly to the line before it about despair, so the two form a pair: collapse under hardship, swagger under relief. The audience included men whose fortunes swung on a single caravan season. No occasion is reported, and the ayah is presented as a description rather than an incident.

keyTerms.note: A verb of tasting, used for a small and temporary experience rather than possession. It quietly contradicts the claim he is about to make, since what you taste has been handed to you.
Three short words with no verb between them, the Arabic shape of a bare ownership claim. Commentators read it as deserved by merit or won by skill, and the phrasing carries both at once.
A feminine superlative used elsewhere of the reward promised to those who do good. Here it sits in the mouth of a man claiming that reward ahead of time, with an emphatic particle attached to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant's life in Mecca swung hard between the two states this ayah describes. A caravan lost to raiders or weather could ruin a family; one that returned full could remake it in a season. Men explained their own successes in the assemblies and were listened to. Attributing a recovered fortune to your own judgement was simply the ordinary way to talk, and it cost nothing socially to do it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase this man uses for the very best appears with an emphatic particle attached, and that exact form occurs only once in the whole Quran, here. Elsewhere the same superlative names what God has promised to those who do good. The construction lets a speaker claim, in a single added syllable of emphasis, a reward the text everywhere else describes as given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates a particular danger in relief rather than in hardship. Hardship at least keeps the question of dependence open; recovery closes it, and the closing is done with a sentence about ownership. What is described is not disbelief argued for but disbelief arrived at through comfort. And the assumption that one would fare well at a reckoning one does not accept shows how little of this was ever reasoned.

crossReferences.why: Puts almost the same claim in the mouth of a man whose wealth was about to be swallowed by the earth.
Combines the same boast with the same doubt about the Hour, in the parable of two garden owners.
Describes the same misreading of both ease and hardship as verdicts God has passed on oneself.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good stretch you are in now, however small, and write one sentence naming where it actually came from. Include at least one person you did not choose and one circumstance you did not arrange. This ayah is not against enjoying it. It is against the sentence that begins with this is mine and then stops there.

studies.title: Turning Aside And Coming Back
studies.meaning: The first line is about the body. Given comfort, the human being turns away and shifts his side off at an angle, a gesture of dismissal rather than a decision reached. Given harm, the same person produces prayer described as wide, spread out, covering everything. Then the surah changes speaker and puts a question. Suppose it really is from God and you rejected it: who is further off the road than someone in a split that has carried him a long way out. No answer is supplied.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the last of three consecutive portraits of the human being under changing fortune, followed by a challenge the Prophet is told to put. Commentators read the sequence as building: first despair, then entitlement, then the physical turning away described here. The closing ayah addresses opponents directly and is phrased as a supposition rather than an assertion, a strategy the Meccan surahs use often.

keyTerms.note: A physical description: shifting the shoulder and body away from someone. Arabic uses it of a person too comfortable to be bothered, and the ayah reports the movement rather than interpreting it.
The adjective for breadth, attached to prayer only here in the Quran. Length would be the expected word. Breadth suggests praying that spreads to cover everything at once, out of alarm.
From the root for splitting a thing in two, used of a schism between parties. It names a position a person occupies rather than an opinion held, which is how distance can be attached to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Body language carried weight in an assembly. Turning the shoulder, sitting sideways, declining to face a speaker were public acts with consequences, read by everyone present and remembered afterwards. A man did not need to announce that he was dismissing you. The gesture named in this ayah was a recognisable social move, which is why the passage describes a posture rather than a thought when it comes to ingratitude.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes prayer here as broad rather than long, and that adjective occurs only in this place. Earlier in the same surah, those in God's presence were described praising Him night and day without ever growing weary. The two portraits sit in one closing section: worship that never stops, and prayer that appears only once something has gone wrong.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates unbelief in a posture before it shows up as an argument. Turning aside happens when nothing is wrong, and the prayer that returns under pressure is not counted as a correction of it. Then the closing challenge shifts the burden. It does not ask the opponent to accept the revelation. It asks him to consider the cost of being wrong about it, which is a different and harder question.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase for the same gesture, and pairs it with the same despair when harm arrives.
Describes the same return under pressure, listing the postures in which the calling gets done.
Opens with the identical supposition, then adds a witness who testified to something like it and believed.

studies.applyIt: Watch your own shoulders this week. When something good arrives, notice whether you turn slightly away from the people and duties around you, a little less available than you were the day before. You do not have to fix it. Just catch the movement once, since this ayah puts the whole diagnosis into a shift of the body.

studies.title: Signs In The Horizons And In Themselves
studies.meaning: A promise of future evidence, given in two locations at once: on the horizons, out at the edges of the known world, and inside the people themselves. Commentators read the horizons as coming events, or as the natural world at large, and the souls as a person's own making and history; the range is recorded rather than resolved. Then a question undercuts the whole apparatus of proof. Is your Lord's being witness over everything not already enough.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the closing two ayat of the surah, spoken to a community with no visible prospect of vindication. The promise of signs on the horizons was given before anything had happened, which is part of why later readers returned to it so often. Commentators differ over whether the horizons mean geography or events. The surah ends on the doubt of its opponents rather than on their defeat.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the line where sky meets land, used for distant territories. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it names the edge of what a person can see rather than a fixed place.
A reflexive verb, so the clarity emerges from the thing itself rather than being supplied by an explainer. What is promised is not persuasion but a becoming-evident that takes its own time.
From the root for a surrounding wall. It closes the surah with an image of enclosure rather than of height, so that nothing is left described as beyond reach or outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The horizon was a working concept for people whose lives depended on what lay past it. Caravans left for Syria and Yemen and returned with news months later, and a merchant's picture of the world was assembled from what travellers had seen. The edge of the known was a real edge. Promising signs out there meant promising something the audience would hear about second hand, and eventually did.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for horizons in this passage occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and the closing word for encompassing appears in this exact form only twice. The surah's final sentence is built as a matched pair: two short clauses, each opened by the same attention-calling particle, one naming the doubt of the opponents and the other naming what surrounds them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage promises evidence and then asks whether evidence was ever the issue. If God's witnessing everything is already sufficient, then what the horizons will show is confirmation for people who had other reasons to doubt. That order matters for a reader: the signs are real and are coming, but they are not the ground belief is being rested on here. The last word of the surah is enclosure, not proof.

crossReferences.why: Pairs the same two locations, the earth and your own selves, as the places where signs are to be found.
Points at the outer half of that pair, and names the kind of person the signs actually reach.
Repeats the outer and inner pairing at the opening of a later surah, adding the creatures scattered about.

studies.applyIt: Take one claim you hold about yourself that you have never checked against evidence, good or bad. Ask someone who has known you five years whether they see it. This passage promises signs in the horizons and in yourself. The second location is the one you can actually go and look at this week, and it takes one conversation.
